HuYgTa-190774-d1e111.summary: Rubric announcing a clear division of Distinctions 24 and 25, in which faith is treated both as it regards its object and as it regards its subject.
claims: Distinctions 24-25 consider faith in relation to its object and to its subject.

HuYgTa-190774-d1e129.summary: A divisio textus for Distinctions 24 and 25. After treating faith absolutely in d. 23, the Master treats it comparatively. Distinction 24 compares faith to what is believed (its object): he removes two objections by showing that faith concerns things unseen, past or present, and then asks whether faith can concern things known. Distinction 25 compares faith to believers (its subject) and to their other virtues and works. On believers, he shows that there was never salvation without faith in the Mediator and asks what the ancients had to believe for salvation, both generally and in the case of the simple and unlearned, adding the particular case of Cornelius after Christ's coming. On the virtues, he states the equality of the theological virtues and their works, raises an objection and resolves it. The paragraph then announces the specific question.
claims: Distinction 24 treats faith in relation to its object, showing it concerns things not seen.
Distinction 25 treats faith in relation to believers, holding that salvation was never possible without faith in the Mediator.
The Master also asks what the ancients, including the simple, had to believe explicitly for salvation.

HuYgTa-190774.summary: The circa textum for Book 3, Distinctions 24 and 25, which are treated together. The divisio textus shows the Master moving from faith considered absolutely (d. 23) to faith considered comparatively: in d. 24 with respect to its object, defending the claim that faith is of things unseen and asking whether it can concern things known; in d. 25 with respect to believers, on the necessity of faith in the Mediator for salvation in every age, the explicit content required of the ancients and of the simple, the case of Cornelius, and the equality of the theological virtues. It introduces the question whether falsehood can underlie faith.
claims: Distinctions 24-25 treat faith comparatively, with respect to its object and its subjects.
Salvation was never possible without faith in the Mediator.
